sourceInformation.genre: Surgical action (a pointer-precision arcade game under a ticking clock), framed by a visual-novel medical melodrama, with drop-in co-op
sourceInformation.perspective: Operations: a fixed surgeon's-eye view of the operative field, 73 degrees from the horizon, with short camera pushes. Story: a staged paper theatre, straight on, plus 3D wide shots of the operating room
sourceInformation.tech: Pavilion engine (shardfall repository, commit 49ef2ba, changed for this game): Rust 1.98.1, wgpu 30 on WebGPU, egui 0.36, rapier 0.36, glam 0.33, cpal 0.18, gilrs 0.11, winit 0.30, WebAssembly, one HTML file. AI Hub session client 1.4.0
sourceInformation.artDirection: The engine's cel bands, ink outlines and bloom. The field is one mesh painted by per-vertex colour with stylised tissue; instruments and parasites are SDF solids; story characters are layered, extruded spline cards like a motion comic. Barlow Condensed for all text. No image or model files
sourceInformation.animation: The engine's sim-driven procedural motion and its puppet clips for the wide shots, plus new procedural animation: instruments squeezing and plunging, tissue beating on the heartbeat, parasites stepping on the beat, paper rigs that blink, breathe, sway and flap their mouths
sourceInformation.audio: All written in code in a bus mixer: about 40 effect cues, a note sequencer with composed tracks whose tempo follows the heart, a crisis layer and a motif per strain in its own meter (3/4, 6/8, 5/4, 7/8), and Animalese-style formant voices per character. Music defaults to 10%
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub Session Protocol v1: one Code Blue round in shared-world mode, 1 to 4 seats, host authoritative, the game's own card. Outside a session the game is unaffected. Local co-op for up to 4 pads
sourceInformation.testing: Headless Rust tests (rules, bot on every case and the whole campaign, coverage, balance targets, determinism, shell navigation, audio rendered offline) and scripted browser tests in Chromium with software WebGPU (stub DualSense, phone profile, analyser tap, hub harness, two-copy and four-copy sessions), plus the whole campaign played in the page through the stub pad and through real mouse and key events, behind one command. Screenshots only for what scripts cannot check. No subagents or workflows
sourceInformation.research: Done by the plan: Trauma Center: Second Opinion (Atlus, Wii launch title, 2006), an enhanced remake of the DS Under the Knife; pointer aiming and Nunchuk flick tool-select; two doctors with different gifts; rank scoring; later New Blood added co-op. No further research by me

testingFeedback: About 35. The ones that mattered: the tumor's ring cut was never spawned, so Case 3 could not be finished; the closing dressing locked out the IV, so a low-vitals player was stuck until death; touch taps missed the Settings button because the canvas was not sized the way the pointer events assumed; slow frames kept hub copies from calling ready in time; the title clipped on a phone; the attract timer ran slow on slow frames; menu repeats overshot on stalled frames; the campaign never used the IV; glasses hid the eyes; the wide-shot camera sat behind a wall. Found late, from a table of every difficulty and skill: pumping the IV paid more than surgery, so slow play ranked above good play; slow bots swapped tools without finishing anything; bursts in Case 4 drained faster than the IV could heal, which made it harder than the final case; and freezing every ember first skipped the merge twist in Case 6. Plus a dozen balance and test-harness fixes.

4: the unfinishable Case 3 tumor, the dressing lock, phone taps missing the only button on that screen, and four-player hub rounds failing the harness. The IV score farm broke the ranks, not the game, so I don't count it here.

The bot playing every case and the whole campaign with coverage counters, together with the balance tool. It runs in seconds, found the unfinishable case and the dressing lock, and told me what to change after every rule edit. Printing wins and times per difficulty and skill, rather than only pass or fail against targets, is what exposed the score farm and the difficulty spike.

Browser tests that waited on real time before I made them count frames: software WebGPU on this busy machine ran at about 1 to 10 frames a second, so they mostly measured the machine. The WebKit iPhone load also told me little, because it stops at the page's WebGPU message.
engineFeedback: Everything runs and draws headless. A deterministic sim behind one small hook, `pav capture` for a real frame in about a second, and `DynamicMesh` plus SDF solids meant I could paint a whole beating organ and see it without a display.

Yes, in small ways. Leftover events from the last scene turned into wild distortions in my first captures, which looked like a rendering bug. I guessed the story camera's distance and put it behind a wall. A new dependency needs one build without --locked. And big release compiles were killed for memory on this shared machine until I built with fewer jobs from a script that waits for free memory.

The game's own frame path and shell in product.rs and pav_ui: focus-list menus, prompts that follow the device, per-pad input with analog triggers, the HUD, and the hub bridge. The plate renderer and the bus mixer with its sequencer and formant voices came next.

Getting out of the demo's way. App::frame carries about 800 lines of demo behaviour, and there is no per-game camera, sound or UI seam, so a game that wants its own screens has to branch above all of it and reopen several crates.

input.rs: surgeon slots and a game command in InputFrame, for replays and co-op. frame.rs and sim.rs: a Cue event and a per-game frame, because the hook cannot draw. build.rs: a per-game emit at the end of the build. session.rs and headless.rs: the game's camera and shell, so the tools see what the window sees. pav_audio: three buses, formant filters, vibrato, a raised voice limit, cues, music and voices. app.rs, simhost.rs and settings.rs: a branch to the game's own frame path and a command queue. pack_single_html.py and index.html: the hub client, tags, shim and About block.

Give games a real seam for their own frame: a trait with camera, draw, sound and UI hooks that the window and the headless tools both call, with the demo's behaviour living behind it instead of in App::frame.
promptFeedback: The plan's check marks. Knowing which values, look and protocol shape had already been tried on this machine saved a great deal of searching, and the plan's clear Never cut list made every trade-off easy.

Mostly small things: the task lets me pick genre and perspective while the plan fixes them, and the plan says it never names the deliverable while its build line needs one. The first was settled by the plan's own note that the task's requirements win.

Passing the hub harness with four software-rendered copies on a shared machine with little free memory, because the protocol's deadlines do not wait for slow frames. The sheer breadth was the other: a whole game, engine seams, audio, co-op and tools in one run.

State a memory budget for builds and browsers alongside the port rules, since other agents compete for it. And say whether a hub round must pass on software rendering, because that drove real design decisions such as the keepalive and the draw throttle.

aiHub.name: Diorama Center: Second Opinion
aiHub.description: Race a failing heart with eight instruments while the patient's pulse sets the tempo of everything, in a rain-soaked harbour hospital where a man-made parasite keeps time. A surgical action melodrama, with up to four surgeons in Code Blue.
aiHub.controls: Right stick or mouse aims, R2 or left click operates, left stick or 1-8 picks tools
